Between 1881 and 1925 European diplomats often used the language of peace, but most agreements before 1914 were really about protecting individual states against specific rivals, and they ended up dividing Europe into armed blocs. After the destruction of the First World War the purpose shifted somewhat. Versailles was still shaped by the winners' interests, but Locarno was a more genuine attempt at collective security, although even it served the national interests of France and Germany.

The background to these agreements is the change in the balance of power after German unification in 1871. A new, powerful Germany in the center of Europe worried its neighbors, and France wanted revenge for losing Alsace-Lorraine. Bismarck tried to keep France isolated by tying the other great powers to Germany. At the same time, the New Imperialism made the powers compete for colonies and influence in Africa and Asia, so diplomacy was not only about European borders but also about empire. This competition explains why so many treaties talked about "interests."

The Three Emperors' League of 1881 (Doc 1) seems peaceful at first, because it promises "benevolent neutrality" and the "localization of the conflict." But the treaty was secret, which shows it was not meant to reassure Europe as a whole. Its real purpose for Germany was to keep Russia and Austria-Hungary from fighting each other in the Balkans and to keep France without allies. The clause about taking "account of their respective interests in the Balkan Peninsula" shows that the main concern was the interests of the three empires. Bismarck kept this up with the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887, but when it was allowed to lapse in 1890, Russia was left free to look for a new partner.

That partner was France. The Franco-Russian Military Convention of 1892 (Doc 2) is defensive in wording, since it only applies "if France is attacked by Germany." However, it was written by the French and Russian general staffs, so it reflects military thinking more than diplomatic thinking. Military officers were focused on winning a war, not preventing one, which is why the treaty says both countries will mobilize "immediately and simultaneously" as soon as any Triple Alliance power mobilizes. This made a local crisis much more likely to turn into a general war, which is what happened in 1914.

The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 (Doc 3) complicates the picture. By drawing a line across Persia that Britain would not cross for concessions, it reduced the old imperial rivalry between Britain and Russia, so in a way it did preserve peace between those two. But it did this by dividing up another country's economy for their own benefit, and it also helped bring Britain closer to the France and Russia bloc. So peace and self-interest overlapped here instead of being opposites.

After the war, the Treaty of Versailles (Doc 4) assigned "the responsibility of Germany and her allies" for the war in Article 231. The winners claimed this was about justice and security, but it also served their interest in getting reparations, even though Article 232 admits Germany's resources were "not adequate" to pay everything. Orpen's painting (Doc 5) shows the signing in the Hall of Mirrors, the same place where the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871, under gilded decoration and the inscription "Le roy gouverne." As a British official war artist, Orpen was presenting the victors' ceremony, and the setting itself was a message of French triumph over Germany. Wilhelm II's memoirs (Doc 6) show the German side of this resentment. Writing in exile after abdicating, he had a reason to blame England's jealousy of German "peaceful penetration" of markets instead of German policy, so his account is self-serving, but it does show how national economic rivalry was behind prewar tensions.

Locarno in 1925 (Doc 7) is different because it was public and included defeated Germany as an equal partner. Germany and France promised they would "in no case attack or invade each other," and the powers "collectively" guaranteed the borders. Still, it only guaranteed Germany's western frontiers, not the eastern ones, which suited Germany's interests.

Overall, the agreements from 1881 to 1914 mainly advanced state interests under defensive language, while the postwar agreements moved, unevenly, toward real collective security.

Between 1762 and 1914, ideas about women's equality changed a great deal, but the legal position of women changed much less. Writers like Wollstonecraft and Mill attacked the idea that women were naturally meant to obey men, and by the late 1800s these arguments had turned into organized mass movements. However, the movements were divided over methods, and by 1914 most European women still could not vote in national elections, so the change was mostly in ideas and organization and only partly in law.

The debate over women took place in a wider context of Enlightenment arguments about natural rights and reason. Thinkers argued that all men had rights by nature, and the French Revolution put these ideas into practice for men, but not for women. Later, industrialization helped spread the ideology of separate spheres, where middle class men worked in public and women were supposed to stay in the home. At the same time, Britain expanded the vote to more men in 1832, 1867 and 1884, which made it more obvious that women were left out because of their sex and not because of property.

At the start of the period, the main idea was that women were naturally inferior and should please men. Rousseau in Document 1 says woman is "made to please and to be in subjection to man," and that her "strength is in her charms." Rousseau was writing a book on education, so his purpose was to tell readers how girls should be raised, and this is important because he was not just describing women but trying to shape how they were trained to think. Wollstonecraft in Document 2 answers him directly, saying she wants women to have power "not over men; but over themselves." She argues that education and reason would make women better members of society. Her point is a big change in ideas, but it did not change laws right away.

By the middle of the 1800s, the arguments became more political. Mill in Document 3 says the "legal subordination of one sex to the other" is "wrong in itself" and should be replaced by "perfect equality." Mill had been a member of Parliament, and in 1867 he proposed an amendment to give women the vote, which was defeated. This shows that even a famous thinker inside Parliament could not change the law, and Mill himself admits in the document that opinions "rooted in the feelings" are hard to change by argument. Engels in Document 4 gives a different view, saying the oppression of women by men was the "first class oppression." Because Engels was a German socialist writing after Marx's death, his purpose was to connect women's problems to private property and class, so for him the vote alone would not free women. This shows that not everyone agreed on what women's liberation meant.

By the early 1900s, ideas turned into large organized movements. Fawcett in Document 6 says the National Union had 305 societies by 1911 and was "constantly and rapidly increasing." As president of the peaceful NUWSS, Fawcett wants to present her group as orderly and successful, and she even claims the movement had both "order" and "audacity," which may be a way to include the militants without endorsing them. Pankhurst in Document 7 disagrees, saying the old leaders were "content with expressions of sympathy" and that the WSPU motto was "Deeds, not words." Writing her autobiography in 1914, she wants to justify the militant tactics her group used. The poster in Document 5 shows uneven scales and says "Justice demands the vote," which was meant to persuade the public that women were treated unfairly.

Even with all this activity, the legal results were limited. Some laws did change, such as the British Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 that let married women keep their own property, and Finland gave women the vote in 1906. But Britain did not give women the vote until after the war, and in France the Napoleonic Code still kept wives under their husbands' authority. Overall, ideas and movements changed how people thought about women and created powerful campaigns, but by 1914 the law in most of Europe had only partly caught up.

Between 1450 and 1789, religious change and conflict greatly transformed the relationship between religious and political authority, because power over the church moved away from the pope and toward kings and princes. However, this transformation was not complete. Rulers took control of churches, but for most of the period they still believed that one shared religion was needed to keep a state stable, and real toleration only came slowly, usually for practical reasons rather than out of principle. The Reformation broke the pope's authority, the wars of religion forced rulers to make settlements, and later the Enlightenment pushed some monarchs toward limited toleration.

Even before Luther, the authority of the papacy was weakening. During the Avignon papacy and the Great Schism, there were at times two or even three men claiming to be pope, which made many people question the church's leadership. Thinkers like Jan Hus in Bohemia criticized church corruption, and the conciliar movement argued that church councils should have authority over the pope. At the same time, monarchs in places like France and Spain were building stronger territorial states and wanted more control over church appointments and money. The printing press also let new religious ideas spread quickly. All of this meant that when Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses in 1517, there were rulers ready to use religious reform to increase their own power.

The clearest change was that political rulers began to take over religious authority directly. In England, Henry VIII wanted an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, and when the pope would not give it, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, making the king the head of the Church of England. This shows that the king, not Rome, now had final authority over religion in England. In the Holy Roman Empire, the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 allowed each prince to choose whether his territory would be Lutheran or Catholic, which is the idea of "cuius regio, eius religio." This settlement put religious choice in the hands of political rulers, and it showed that conflict between Catholics and Lutherans had made it impossible for the emperor or the pope to force one faith on everyone.

However, these changes did not mean the end of the idea that a state needed one religion. Augsburg did not give toleration to individuals, and it left out Calvinists completely, which helped lead to the Thirty Years' War. Catholic states also show continuity. The kings of France and Spain gained a lot of control over their churches without ever breaking with Rome, so increasing state power over religion was not only a Protestant development. In France, Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, giving Huguenots limited rights to worship, but this was a compromise to end the wars of religion, not a belief in toleration. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685 because he believed in "one king, one law, one faith," and many Huguenots fled the country. This shows that the old belief in religious unity was still strong more than a century after the Reformation started.

Change did continue later in the period. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 recognized Calvinism and largely ended the era of major religious wars, and after this, religion became less of a reason for wars between states. In the eighteenth century, Enlightenment writers like Voltaire attacked religious persecution, and Joseph II of Austria issued a Patent of Toleration in 1781 that gave Protestants and Orthodox Christians more rights. Still, even this toleration was granted from above by a ruler who kept control over the church, so it actually shows how much power the state now had over religion.
